required_units.text: Space for your own cycle or review record, questions and notes, followed by your treatment card.
Carboplatin · 21-day breast scheduleNational Cancer Control Programme (NCCP) 00261

Record each cycle separately. Each medicine has its own symptom table. Mark the worst symptoms since your last review, when they occurred and what they stopped you doing. Overlapping symptoms can be recorded under more than one medicine; you do not have to identify the cause.

These are patient-language severity prompts, not a validated questionnaire or a formal Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) grading tool. Your team assigns the clinical grade. Serious symptoms override the columns: call without waiting to decide a severity level.
Use a new record sheet for each cycle or review. Copy or print another sheet when needed; the number of sheets does not prescribe the length of treatment.
Carboplatin · 21-day breast schedule · reusable record · copy this sheet for another cycle of the same phase.
□ Tiredness improves with rest
□ Rest does not help; usual tasks affected: call
□ Self-care difficult: urgent review
□ Queasy but eating and drinking
□ Intake reduced: contact the team
□ Unable to maintain intake: urgent review
□ Collapse / severe dehydration: 112/999
□ New small bruise / brief bleed: report
□ Repeated bleeding: call today
□ Bleeding that will not stop: urgent help
□ Heavy bleeding / collapse: 112/999
□ Mild change; usual tasks unaffected
□ Limits buttons, writing or walking: call
□ Washing, dressing or walking difficult: urgent review
□ Sudden major weakness / paralysis: emergency help

unique_source_inventory.text: Severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or severe chest pain: call emergency services. Do not wait for an online answer.

Temperature 37.5°C or higher, 36°C or lower, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell — even with a normal temperature. Contact the oncology emergency service immediately for fever or shaking chills, sudden illness, bleeding, new breathlessness, chest pain or severe allergy. Report reduced urine, hearing changes and new numbness promptly. Do not wait for the next visit.

Follow the urgent contact instructions from your treating hospital. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Outside clinic hours, use your instructed out-of-hours pathway or the emergency department.
This page does not diagnose symptoms or decide whether it is safe to stay at home. You do not need to know which medicine caused a symptom before calling.
Aim to slow or shrink metastatic breast cancer and help symptoms, balancing possible benefit, side effects and treatment burden.

Carboplatin forms links in DNA that interfere with DNA copying and repair. This can stop cancer cells dividing. Normal blood-forming cells can also be affected, and kidney function determines how the medicine is cleared.

What to watch forContact the oncology emergency service immediately for fever or shaking chills, sudden illness, bleeding, new breathlessness, chest pain or severe allergy. Report reduced urine, hearing changes and new numbness promptly. Do not wait for the next visit.

There are no guaranteed “safe days”. A day without treatment is not automatically a safe day. Use the emergency contact when needed; do not move or restart doses yourself.

Carboplatin is infused on Day 1 of each 21-day cycle. The team selects the dose using the prescribed AUC and kidney function. Treatment continues while helpful and tolerated; there is no fixed breast course length. Follow the written plan from your treatment team; no dates are entered here.
One infusion visit per 21-day cycle plus pre-cycle blood tests and clinical review. Additional tests depend on symptoms and the individual plan.
Your team chooses venous access. A port is optional, requires a separate insertion procedure and later removal; it is not removed after every infusion.
Allow time for blood review, preparation, anti-sickness treatment, the infusion and observation. No take-home infusion pump is part of this regimen.
Keep emergency contacts, medicine lists and the next appointment plan. Report line redness, swelling, leakage, pain or fever promptly.

Carboplatin is given through a vein over about 30 minutes after blood and symptom review and prescribed anti-sickness medicines. The complete appointment takes longer. A cannula or existing line may be used; a port is not automatically required.

Take the prescribed anti-sickness medicines before treatment and on the following days, even if you feel well. Follow your own prescription and contact the team if nausea or vomiting is not controlled.
Keep blood tests and use the emergency contact for fever, chills or bleeding. Preventive growth-factor injections depend on individual risk.
Tell the team about every medicine or supplement, especially treatments that affect kidneys, hearing or bleeding. Follow individual drinking advice.
The anti-sickness plan may affect sleep, glucose and bowel symptoms. Confirm the exact doses and last day of each medicine; contact the team if symptoms persist.
Advanced breast cancer. This patient suite describes the breast setting; the source protocol also has other tumour indications with their own clinical context.

Carboplatin for metastatic breast cancer is an off-label use under this Irish NCCP protocol. The treating team must explain this, obtain informed consent and follow local Drugs and Therapeutics Committee approval requirements.
Every dose depends on the reviewed treatment plan and results.
Kidney dosing, hearing and nerve review are central. Scans follow the consultant plan; no universal heart-scan schedule is specified.

Discuss fertility preservation before treatment if relevant. Carboplatin may affect periods and fertility, sometimes permanently. Do not breastfeed during treatment. Discuss reliable contraception and contact the team immediately if pregnancy is possible. The linked Irish SmPC advises effective contraception for women during treatment and at least 6 months afterwards; men should avoid fathering a child during treatment and at least 3 months afterwards. Confirm the actual product/local advice and any longer requirement from other medicines. Discuss low blood counts and sepsis, bleeding, nausea/vomiting, fatigue, kidney, hearing and nerve effects, and infusion allergy. Benefit is uncertain and alternatives depend on your cancer and priorities.

If the team calculates kidney function from a blood creatinine result, the NCCP plan requires that result within 48 hours before carboplatin. If a measured kidney scan is used, a rise in creatinine can require a new dose calculation or kidney measurement. The team checks the method, trend and prescribed dose; do not calculate or change the dose yourself.
Keep the written medicine and urgent-contact plan.

In the TNT study of advanced triple-negative or inherited BRCA1/2-associated breast cancer, carboplatin was active, but did not outperform docetaxel in the full study population. The inherited BRCA1/2 subgroup responded more often to carboplatin. These findings help inform a treatment discussion; they do not predict an individual result.
The team considers previous treatment, cancer features, health and your priorities. A response in a trial cannot guarantee benefit for an individual.
No. The consultant selects an AUC target within the source range and the team uses verified kidney function and previous effects to calculate the dose. Do not calculate or change it yourself.

The breast source continues until cancer progression or unacceptable toxicity. The team agrees response reviews and continuation; the fixed course of a particular trial or another cancer type does not set your course.
This carboplatin monotherapy regimen does not mandate routine heart scans. Tests are arranged when symptoms, other medicines or your individual risks make them appropriate.

unique_source_inventory.text: Severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or severe chest pain: call emergency services. Do not wait for an online answer.

Temperature 37.5°C or higher, 36°C or lower, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell — even with a normal temperature. Contact oncology promptly for fever, shivering, sudden illness, unusual bleeding, persistent vomiting, much less urine or inability to drink. Report worsening hearing, numbness or tingling before the next dose. Severe breathing difficulty, collapse or severe chest pain is an emergency.

Follow the urgent contact instructions from your treating hospital. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Outside clinic hours, use your instructed out-of-hours pathway or the emergency department.
This page does not diagnose symptoms or decide whether it is safe to stay at home. You do not need to know which medicine caused a symptom before calling.

Carboplatin is given with radiotherapy to treat locally advanced head and neck cancer when cisplatin is unsuitable. Your team explains the intended chance of cure or long-term control for your diagnosis.

Carboplatin forms links in DNA that interfere with DNA copying and repair. This can stop cancer cells dividing. Normal blood-forming cells can also be affected, and kidney function determines how the medicine is cleared.

What to watch forContact the oncology emergency service immediately for fever or shaking chills, sudden illness, bleeding, new breathlessness, chest pain or severe allergy. Report reduced urine, hearing changes and new numbness promptly. Do not wait for the next visit.

Radiotherapy directs radiation at a carefully planned area. It is delivered on its own appointment calendar. Effects depend on which tissues receive radiation and can build up during the course or continue after it finishes.
What to watch forReport difficulty swallowing, weight loss, mouth pain, skin breakdown or problems managing saliva.

Radiation has its own calendar. Mouth, skin and swallowing effects can build across weeks and continue afterwards. Follow the support plan and contact oncology early if symptoms develop.

Ask for speech and language therapy if swallowing or speech is difficult. Use the food textures, exercises and communication support advised for you; a general guide cannot establish safe swallowing.

Tell staff immediately about itching, a rash, dizziness, chest tightness, breathing difficulty, pain or swelling around the treatment site.

Ask for help before a practical problem prevents treatment.

Your team chooses suitable venous access for an infusion. A port, if used, has its own insertion, care and removal plan; it is not removed after each visit. No take-home chemotherapy pump is part of this regimen.
Discuss transport, work, caring responsibilities, interpreter needs and a support person. Ask how results and changes will be communicated and who books your next tests.
Keep the information that another clinician would need.
Record the cycle received, date, route, dose if supplied, important symptoms, any hold and the next agreed review. Stamp boxes record treatment received; they do not authorise the next dose.

Have the team replace example telephone numbers with your actual daytime and out-of-hours contacts. Carry the front/back wallet card and immune alert card when applicable. The printed handbook contains the key information without needing to scan a QR code.
Bring your main question, changes in swallowing or weight, symptoms, medicine changes and any concerns about the treatment aim. Ask for the plan in words you can explain back.
Use evidence to support a personal treatment discussion.

Pembrolizumab 200 mg · every 3 weeks · lung cancerNational Cancer Control Programme (NCCP) 00455

Record each cycle separately. Each medicine has its own symptom table. Mark the worst symptoms since your last review, when they occurred and what they stopped you doing. Overlapping symptoms can be recorded under more than one medicine; you do not have to identify the cause.

These are patient-language severity prompts, not a validated questionnaire or a formal Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) grading tool. Your team assigns the clinical grade. Serious symptoms override the columns: call without waiting to decide a severity level.
Use a new record sheet for each cycle or review. Copy or print another sheet when needed; the number of sheets does not prescribe the length of treatment.

unique_source_inventory.text: Severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or severe chest pain: call emergency services. Do not wait for an online answer.

Temperature 37.5°C or higher, 36°C or lower, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell — even with a normal temperature. Contact the oncology team immediately for new or worsening breathlessness, chest pain, persistent diarrhoea, severe tummy pain, yellow skin/eyes, much less urine, severe headache, marked weakness, confusion, unusual thirst or passing much more urine, or a spreading/blistering rash. For severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or other immediately dangerous symptoms, seek emergency care. Do not wait for the next infusion.

Follow the urgent contact instructions from your treating hospital. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Outside clinic hours, use your instructed out-of-hours pathway or the emergency department.
This page does not diagnose symptoms or decide whether it is safe to stay at home. You do not need to know which medicine caused a symptom before calling.

For metastatic lung cancer, the aim is to control cancer and help people live longer. After surgery and platinum chemotherapy, the adjuvant aim is to reduce the chance of cancer returning. Ask which aim applies to you.

Pembrolizumab is an antibody that blocks PD-1, a control switch on immune T cells. Cancer cells can use this switch to reduce immune attack. Blocking it can help the immune system recognise and attack cancer. The same increased immune activity can inflame healthy organs, which is why new symptoms need attention even after treatment ends.
What to watch forReport new breathing, bowel, skin, hormone, heart or nerve symptoms promptly; these may be immune inflammation.

There are no guaranteed “safe days”. Immune effects can happen on any day and after treatment ends. Carry your immunotherapy alert card and tell any healthcare team that you receive pembrolizumab.

The team reviews your blood results, symptoms and medicines. Tell the nurse straight away about itching, flushing, a tight chest, dizziness or feeling suddenly unwell during the drip. Before leaving, confirm the next tests, treatment visit and urgent contact number.

You may feel well between infusions, but immune inflammation can begin at any time. Keep a short symptom record and take medicines exactly as prescribed. Contact your team about new symptoms instead of waiting for your next appointment. Confirm thyroid tests are booked every 3–6 weeks, even if infusions are six weeks apart.
Agree the arrangements with your oncology team.
Pembrolizumab 200 mg is given as a drip over about 30 minutes on Day 1 every 3 weeks (21 days). The hospital visit is longer because of checks and preparation.
Blood tests are due before each infusion. Thyroid tests stay every 3–6 weeks regardless of dose schedule. Ask about travel, work, transport and whom to contact if a test or visit is delayed.
Keep the alert card, symptom record, current medicine list and urgent contact details accessible. Your team may prescribe steroids or hormone replacement only if needed.
Keep reporting new symptoms. Some hormone medicines and monitoring continue after the cancer treatment finishes.
Pembrolizumab alone has a minimal risk of causing sickness. Routine anti-sickness medicines or infusion premedicines are not usually needed; your team can prescribe symptom relief if required.
Carry your alert card during treatment and afterwards. Show it when seeking urgent care; symptoms can be mistaken for an infection or an ordinary stomach upset.

Some immune effects need steroids or hormone replacement. Follow the prescribed plan and do not stop steroids suddenly. Ask for help if symptoms worsen or you cannot take essential medicines. If treatment is paused because of an immune side effect, your team checks recovery and any steroid or hormone plan before deciding whether it can restart. Do not change steroids or restart treatment yourself.

Discuss pregnancy, fertility and breastfeeding before treatment. Use effective contraception during treatment and for at least four months after the last dose. If pregnancy is possible or occurs, contact your oncology team promptly.
First confirm which lung setting applies to you.

Metastatic means the cancer has spread. First-line means the first medicine treatment for this stage. Here, pembrolizumab alone is offered for suitable cancers with a high PD-L1 result and without EGFR or ALK alterations. The aim is usually control, symptom relief and more time.

Adjuvant means treatment after surgery to reduce the chance of cancer returning. This pathway follows complete resection and platinum chemotherapy for cancer at high risk of recurrence. It does not use the same high PD-L1 requirement as the metastatic pathway.
Ask which other treatments, clinical trials, surveillance or symptom-focused care fit your exact cancer and health. Supportive care can help during either pathway.
This is an immunotherapy medicine.

The immune system can also attack healthy tissues. Lung, bowel, liver, kidney, skin, gland, heart and nerve inflammation can range from mild to serious. Some hormone changes need long-term replacement.

Your team may delay a dose, treat side effects or stop pembrolizumab. The usual response to immune toxicity is to hold or stop treatment, not to give a smaller dose. Feeling better or having normal tests does not by itself mean that pembrolizumab can restart. Your team reviews what happened, recovery and the steroid or hormone plan. Some reactions mean that treatment must remain stopped, even if the symptoms have settled. Follow the prescribed plan and never restart treatment or change steroids yourself. Restart depends on the original reaction, recovery and any steroid or hormone plan. Some reactions mean treatment must remain stopped even after symptoms settle.
The appointment pattern and total duration are different decisions.
These lung trials used pembrolizumab 200 mg every 3 weeks. Trial treatment limits and research scan schedules are not automatic NCCP prescribing rules.
Tell your team about symptoms even when recent blood tests were normal.

Your team checks the cancer diagnosis, treatment aim and relevant tumour tests. Blood count, kidney/liver, glucose and thyroid tests provide a baseline. Discuss existing illnesses, medicines, pregnancy and breastfeeding.
Blood count, kidney/liver function and glucose before every 3-week cycle; thyroid every 3–6 weeks, cortisol if indicated, and symptom review throughout and after treatment.
Extra tests may be needed for symptoms. Follow the agreed steroid or hormone plan. Keep your alert card and continue reporting symptoms after the last dose.
Keep your team informed about what matters to you.
Fatigue can affect daily activities. Balance activity with rest and ask for help if tiredness is new, marked or accompanied by dizziness, headache, thirst or weakness; it may need medical assessment.
Drink as advised and report ongoing vomiting or diarrhoea. Do not assume diarrhoea is a minor stomach upset; your team needs to check for immune inflammation and other causes.
Bring a full medicine list, including supplements and steroids. Ask before starting new medicines. Use the contraception plan and discuss fertility or breastfeeding with your team.
Use the contact plan given by your oncology service.

Contact the oncology team immediately for new or worsening breathlessness, chest pain, persistent diarrhoea, severe tummy pain, yellow skin/eyes, much less urine, severe headache, marked weakness, confusion, unusual thirst or passing much more urine, or a spreading/blistering rash. For severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or other immediately dangerous symptoms, seek emergency care. Do not wait for the next infusion.
Tell the nurse immediately if you become itchy, flushed, breathless, dizzy, tight-chested or suddenly unwell.
Immune inflammation can start late. Tell any healthcare team about pembrolizumab even after the course has finished.

Heart, muscle and nerve problems can occur together. New muscle pain or weakness with changed vision, unusual tiredness, breathlessness, chest pain or an irregular heartbeat needs immediate medical advice. Do not wait for several symptoms to appear together. Severe breathing difficulty, collapse or rapidly worsening weakness needs emergency care.

In a trial of suitable people with metastatic lung cancer and a high PD-L1 result, pembrolizumab helped people live longer than chemotherapy. After surgery and chemotherapy, a separate trial found a lower risk of recurrence or death. Its final long-term analysis did not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in overall survival. The aims and evidence differ between these settings.
These results describe groups of people, not what will happen to one person. The metastatic and after-surgery studies answer different questions.

Ask your team to write down the treatment aim. For metastatic disease, the aim is usually cancer control, symptom relief and more time. After complete surgery and platinum chemotherapy, adjuvant treatment aims to reduce the chance of recurrence.

For the first-line metastatic monotherapy pathway, the source requires high PD-L1 expression and no EGFR mutation or ALK translocation. The adjuvant pathway has different eligibility. Ask which results apply to your own cancer.

The adjuvant course lasts up to 12 months. Metastatic treatment continues while helpful and tolerable; a 24-month review may lead to stopping or continuing. Symptoms, response and your preferences can change the plan.

The oncology team arranges and reviews tests. Blood count, kidney/liver function and glucose are checked before each cycle; thyroid tests are usually every 3–6 weeks. Ask whether an extra test is needed between six-weekly infusions.

Report new or worsening breathing problems, persistent diarrhoea, severe abdominal pain, yellow eyes, reduced urine, severe headache, weakness, thirst or a spreading rash promptly. Keep the local oncology and out-of-hours numbers available; severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or severe chest pain needs 112 / 999.

Ask about alternatives for your exact stage and tumour results, including other anticancer treatments, trials, surveillance where appropriate and symptom-focused care. Supportive care remains available whether or not you proceed.

Not by itself. Your team checks whether the change is caused by immune inflammation, another medicine, cancer or another illness. They decide whether to pause treatment, investigate further or stop it. Do not change the treatment plan yourself.

unique_source_inventory.text: Severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or severe chest pain: call emergency services. Do not wait for an online answer.

Temperature 37.5°C or higher, 36°C or lower, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell — even with a normal temperature. Contact oncology immediately for new breathlessness, chest pain, diarrhoea, severe tummy pain, yellow skin or eyes, much less urine, severe headache, vision changes, marked weakness, confusion, unusual thirst or a spreading or blistering rash. Severe breathing difficulty, collapse or seizure is an emergency.

Follow the urgent contact instructions from your treating hospital. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Outside clinic hours, use your instructed out-of-hours pathway or the emergency department.
This page does not diagnose symptoms or decide whether it is safe to stay at home. You do not need to know which medicine caused a symptom before calling.
Pembrolizumab aims to control head and neck cancer that has returned or spread, relieve symptoms and help some people live longer. Benefit and side effects are reviewed for you.

Pembrolizumab is an antibody that blocks PD-1, a control switch on immune T cells. Cancer cells can use this switch to reduce immune attack. Blocking it can help the immune system recognise and attack cancer. The same increased immune activity can inflame healthy organs, which is why new symptoms need attention even after treatment ends.
What to watch forReport new breathing, bowel, skin, hormone, heart or nerve symptoms promptly; these may be immune inflammation.

This shows treatment timing, not guaranteed symptom-free days. Your team confirms the active phase and dates.

Pembrolizumab 200 mg is given through a vein over about 30 minutes on Day 1 every 3 weeks. The whole visit includes safety checks, preparation and observation. Treatment continues until progression or unacceptable toxicity. After 24 months of sustained response without progression, the team may consider stopping; stopping at 24 months is not automatic.
Treatment continues until progression or unacceptable toxicity. After 24 months of sustained response without progression, the team may consider stopping; stopping at 24 months is not automatic.
These stages are not equal time intervals. Your team provides dates and reviews results. There is no universal blood tumour-marker panel or scan interval in this guide.

Assesses the cancer and the response to treatment separately from safety bloods.

This indication excludes nasopharyngeal cancer and cancer progressing within six months after curatively intended systemic treatment for locoregionally advanced disease.

Pembrolizumab 200 mg is given through a vein over about 30 minutes on Day 1 every 3 weeks. The whole visit includes safety checks, preparation and observation. Report symptoms and previous reactions before treatment.
Immune side effects may start between visits or after the final dose. Report changes promptly. Follow the support plan and contact oncology early if symptoms develop.
Carry your treatment record, actual urgent contacts and medicine list. Tell the team about line redness, swelling, leakage, pain or fever.

Carry your immune alert card during and after pembrolizumab. Tell any clinician that you have received immunotherapy. Do not restart a held treatment or change prescribed steroids or hormone replacement yourself.
Tell the team early if swallowing, appetite, pain or taste changes reduce intake. A dietitian can agree practical food, drink or feeding support with you. Do not wait for substantial weight loss.
Agree a mouth-care plan and tell your dentist about previous or current cancer treatment. Arrange oncology advice before dental procedures, particularly after head and neck radiation.
Ask for speech and language therapy if swallowing or speech is difficult. Use the food textures, exercises and communication support advised for you; a general guide cannot establish safe swallowing.

Bring prescribed, over-the-counter and herbal medicines and supplements for review. Discuss fertility preservation and breastfeeding before treatment. Use effective contraception during treatment and for at least four months after the final dose. Tell the team promptly about a possible pregnancy. Do not breastfeed without specific advice from the team.
Keep your own diagnosis and treatment aim at the front of the plan.

Your team weighs the cancer, previous treatment, health, symptoms and preferences when discussing options. Other systemic treatment, local treatment where suitable, trials or symptom-focused care may be discussed.
Cancer treatment can also affect healthy tissue.
Keep one calendar for treatment, tests and other appointments.
Your team may pause or stop treatment to assess side effects. Record the reason, required tests and who can authorise restarting. A new cycle does not erase earlier severe toxicity.
Blood safety tests, tumour tests and scans answer different questions.
Your team agrees examinations and scans to assess cancer response. No universal scan interval or blood tumour-marker panel is assumed here.

Use the oncology service’s written urgent-contact plan.

Contact oncology immediately for new breathlessness, chest pain, diarrhoea, severe tummy pain, yellow skin or eyes, much less urine, severe headache, vision changes, marked weakness, confusion, unusual thirst or a spreading or blistering rash. Severe breathing difficulty, collapse or seizure is an emergency.
Tell staff immediately about itching, a rash, dizziness, chest tightness, breathing difficulty, pain or swelling around the treatment site.

Tell the clinician the medicine name, date of the last dose, new symptoms and any prescribed steroids or hormone replacement. Carry the wallet card; do not delay urgent care while looking for a document.
Ask for help before a practical problem prevents treatment.
Ask for individual speech and language therapy advice for swallowing or communication difficulties. Report choking, coughing with drinks or inability to swallow safely.
Plan manageable activity and rest around symptoms. Tell the team about severe or unexpected fatigue, falls or difficulties managing at home.
Review medicines and practical needs before treatment.

Your team chooses suitable venous access for an infusion. A port, if used, has its own insertion, care and removal plan; it is not removed after each visit. No take-home chemotherapy pump is part of this regimen.
Discuss transport, work, caring responsibilities, interpreter needs and a support person. Ask how results and changes will be communicated and who books your next tests.
Keep the information that another clinician would need.
Record the cycle received, date, route, dose if supplied, important symptoms, any hold and the next agreed review. Stamp boxes record treatment received; they do not authorise the next dose.

Have the team replace example telephone numbers with your actual daytime and out-of-hours contacts. Carry the front/back wallet card and immune alert card when applicable. The printed handbook contains the key information without needing to scan a QR code.
Bring your main question, changes in swallowing or weight, symptoms, medicine changes and any concerns about the treatment aim. Ask for the plan in words you can explain back.
Use evidence to support a personal treatment discussion.

KEYNOTE-048 supports pembrolizumab alone in the PD-L1-positive first-line recurrent or metastatic population. It compared treatment groups, not an individual prognosis. The trial used 200 mg every three weeks; the six-week schedule is not a separate randomised head and neck survival comparison.
Group results cannot predict what will happen for you. Ask which benefits matter for your situation and how the team will decide whether treatment remains worthwhile.
The source list gives the official regimen and public patient information. Ask your team for a printed copy or help accessing a resource if needed.

Nivolumab · every 2 weeks · previously treated non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC)National Cancer Control Programme (NCCP) 00483

Record each cycle separately. Each medicine has its own symptom table. Mark the worst symptoms since your last review, when they occurred and what they stopped you doing. Overlapping symptoms can be recorded under more than one medicine; you do not have to identify the cause.

These are patient-language severity prompts, not a validated questionnaire or a formal Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) grading tool. Your team assigns the clinical grade. Serious symptoms override the columns: call without waiting to decide a severity level.
Use a new record sheet for each cycle or review. Copy or print another sheet when needed; the number of sheets does not prescribe the length of treatment.

unique_source_inventory.text: Severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or severe chest pain: call emergency services. Do not wait for an online answer.

Temperature 37.5°C or higher, 36°C or lower, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell — even with a normal temperature. Contact the oncology team immediately for new or worsening breathlessness, chest pain, persistent diarrhoea, severe tummy pain, yellow skin/eyes, much less urine, severe headache, marked weakness, confusion, unusual thirst or passing much more urine, or a spreading/blistering rash. For severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or other immediately dangerous symptoms, seek emergency care. Do not wait for the next infusion.

Follow the urgent contact instructions from your treating hospital. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Outside clinic hours, use your instructed out-of-hours pathway or the emergency department.
This page does not diagnose symptoms or decide whether it is safe to stay at home. You do not need to know which medicine caused a symptom before calling.
Aim to control advanced lung cancer, relieve symptoms and prolong life where possible.
Nivolumab blocks PD-1 on immune cells, helping them recognise and attack cancer. It can also cause inflammation in healthy organs.
What to watch forReport new breathing, bowel, skin, hormone, heart or nerve symptoms promptly; these may be immune inflammation.
The drawings are simplified explanations of drug action, not anatomical pictures or a prediction of response.
This shows treatment timing, not guaranteed symptom-free days. Your team confirms the active phase and dates.

Nivolumab 240 mg IV over 30 minutes OR 600 mg as a subcutaneous injection over 3–5 minutes on Day 1 every 2 weeks. Your team confirms one formulation; the whole visit includes checks and preparation. Continue until progression or unacceptable toxicity, with individual benefit and safety review.
There is no planned chemotherapy induction or maintenance switch in this monotherapy pathway. Treatment is reviewed regularly and may be held, stopped or changed.
This is a relative treatment map, not a booking calendar. Ask who books each test and reviews the result. Extra tests may be needed for symptoms.

There are no guaranteed “safe days”. Immune effects can happen on any day and after treatment ends. Carry your immunotherapy alert card and tell any healthcare team that you receive nivolumab.

The team checks blood results, symptoms and medicines before the prescribed infusion or injection. Tell the nurse immediately about itching, flushing, breathlessness, dizziness or feeling suddenly unwell. Before leaving, confirm the next tests, treatment visit and urgent contact number.

You may feel well between infusions, but immune inflammation can begin at any time. Keep a short symptom record and take medicines exactly as prescribed. Contact your team about new symptoms instead of waiting for your next appointment. Confirm monthly thyroid tests and who arranges them; report new symptoms without waiting for the next treatment.
Agree the arrangements with your oncology team.
Nivolumab 240 mg IV over 30 minutes OR 600 mg as a subcutaneous injection over 3–5 minutes on Day 1 every 2 weeks. Your team confirms one formulation; the whole visit includes checks and preparation.
Continue until progression or unacceptable toxicity, with individual benefit and safety review.

Blood count, kidney/liver tests and glucose before every 2-week cycle; thyroid once a month; cortisol if clinically indicated. Review cancer progression before cycle 8. Continue immune-toxicity monitoring for at least 5 months after the last dose.
Carry your immune alert card, medicine list and urgent contact details. Follow prescribed steroids or hormone replacement carefully; do not stop steroids suddenly.
Keep reporting symptoms and attend agreed follow-up for at least 5 months after the final dose; some hormone replacement continues longer.
Nivolumab alone has minimal sickness risk. Routine preventive anti-sickness medicines or premedication are not usually required; the team may prescribe symptom relief.
Carry your alert card during treatment and afterwards. Show it when seeking urgent care; symptoms can be mistaken for an infection or an ordinary stomach upset.

Some immune effects need steroids or hormone replacement. Follow the prescribed plan and do not stop steroids suddenly. Ask for help if symptoms worsen or you cannot take essential medicines. Hormone replacement alone does not always mean nivolumab must stop. Your team checks symptoms and recovery and reviews any medicines that suppress the immune system before deciding whether treatment can continue or restart.

Discuss pregnancy, fertility and breastfeeding before treatment. Use effective contraception during treatment and for at least 5 months after the last dose. Breastfeeding requires a specialist decision; contact your team promptly if pregnancy occurs.
Adults with locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC after prior chemotherapy; recurrence or progression during or after one prior platinum-containing doublet for advanced/metastatic disease; ECOG 0–1.
Discuss other treatment, trials and symptom-focused care with your team.
Immunotherapy supports immune attack.
Nivolumab blocks PD-1 on immune cells, helping them recognise and attack cancer. It can also cause the immune system to inflame healthy organs.
Inflammation can affect lungs, bowel, liver, kidneys, skin, glands, muscles, heart and nerves. Some effects are serious, delayed or permanent.
Confirm the formulation with your team.
Treatment may be held or stopped for side effects. Nivolumab is not routinely dose-reduced. Tell the team about missed appointments.

If your team has permanently stopped nivolumab because of a serious immune reaction, improvement does not automatically make restarting safe. Keep that decision in your treatment record; only your specialist team can review further treatment.
New symptoms matter even when recent tests were normal.
Blood count, kidney/liver tests, glucose and thyroid tests establish a baseline; discuss existing illness and all medicines.
Your team assesses progression before cycle 8; later scans follow the consultant plan.
Tell your team what matters to you.
Balance activity and rest. New marked fatigue with dizziness, headache, thirst or weakness needs assessment.
Bring all medicine/supplement details. Discuss fertility and breastfeeding. Use effective contraception during treatment and for at least 5 months after the final dose.
Minimal sickness risk: routine preventive sickness medicines are not usually required. Your team may prescribe symptom relief.
Use your oncology urgent contact plan.

Report new breathlessness, persistent diarrhoea, severe pain, yellow eyes, reduced urine, severe headache, weakness, unusual thirst or a spreading/blistering rash immediately. Use your oncology contact plan; severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or severe chest pain needs emergency care.
Tell the nurse immediately about a reaction during the infusion or injection.
Continue monitoring for at least 5 months after the final dose. Show your immune alert card to anyone treating you.
Nivolumab can help the immune system control some previously treated lung cancers. Some people benefit for a long time; others do not benefit.
Trial results describe groups, not an individual prognosis.

Previously treated locally advanced or metastatic non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC). It is used after previous chemotherapy to help control cancer; ask how the benefits and alternatives apply to you.
Ask about other anticancer treatment, trials and symptom-focused care suited to your cancer and preferences. Support remains available if you decline treatment.

Minimal emetic risk; no routine antiemetic prophylaxis or premedication. Prescribe rescue/support individually.
Immune alert card and immediate symptom reporting.
Effective contraception during treatment and at least 5 months afterwards; specialist breastfeeding discussion.
Current NCIS medical-oncology guidance does not create a routine cytotoxic prescription for minimal-risk nivolumab monotherapy.

Hormone replacement alone does not always mean nivolumab must stop. Your team checks symptoms and recovery and reviews any medicines that suppress the immune system before deciding whether treatment can continue or restart.

A previous permanent-stop decision remains part of the nivolumab treatment history even if symptoms improve; do not restart without specialist review. Keep the agreed steroid, other immunosuppression and hormone plan.

Carry your immune alert card during and after nivolumab. Tell any clinician that you have received immunotherapy. Do not restart a held treatment or change prescribed steroids or hormone replacement yourself.
Tell the team early if swallowing, appetite, pain or taste changes reduce intake. A dietitian can agree practical food, drink or feeding support with you. Do not wait for substantial weight loss.
Agree a mouth-care plan and tell your dentist about previous or current cancer treatment. Arrange oncology advice before dental procedures, particularly after head and neck radiation.
Ask for speech and language therapy if swallowing or speech is difficult. Use the food textures, exercises and communication support advised for you; a general guide cannot establish safe swallowing.

Your team may pause or stop treatment to assess side effects. Record the reason, required tests and who can authorise restarting. A new cycle does not erase earlier severe toxicity.

When switching from two-week to four-week dosing, the first four-week dose is given two weeks after the last two-week dose. In the reverse direction, the first two-week dose is given four weeks after the last four-week dose. Your team confirms the actual switch date and formulation.

Intravenous treatment needs suitable venous access. Under-the-skin nivolumab is given into the thigh or abdomen, rotating sites and avoiding damaged skin, scars and moles. It is not given into a vein. Tell staff about local pain or swelling.
Discuss transport, work, caring responsibilities, interpreter needs and a support person. Ask how results and changes will be communicated and who books your next tests.

Record each cycle separately. Each medicine has its own symptom table. Mark the worst symptoms since your last review, when they occurred and what they stopped you doing. Overlapping symptoms can be recorded under more than one medicine; you do not have to identify the cause.

These are patient-language severity prompts, not a validated questionnaire or a formal Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) grading tool. Your team assigns the clinical grade. Serious symptoms override the columns: call without waiting to decide a severity level.
Use a new record sheet for each cycle or review. Copy or print another sheet when needed; the number of sheets does not prescribe the length of treatment.

rows.label: Nivolumab treatment
rows.text: Nivolumab is given as 240 mg by IV infusion over 30 minutes OR 600 mg by subcutaneous injection over 3–5 minutes, on Day 1 every 2 weeks. Allow extra time for assessment, preparation and observation. The team selects one formulation. A subcutaneous injection is given into the thigh or abdomen, alternating sites and avoiding damaged skin, scars or moles. IV and subcutaneous doses are not interchangeable milligram for milligram.

unique_source_inventory.text: Severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or severe chest pain: call emergency services. Do not wait for an online answer.

Temperature 37.5°C or higher, 36°C or lower, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell — even with a normal temperature. Immunotherapy can cause inflammation in healthy organs during treatment or after it stops. Contact the oncology team promptly for new diarrhoea, blood in stools, cough or breathlessness, yellow skin or eyes, severe headache, vision changes, marked thirst, unusual weakness or a spreading rash. Tell any clinician that you are receiving or have received immunotherapy.

Follow the urgent contact instructions from your treating hospital. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Outside clinic hours, use your instructed out-of-hours pathway or the emergency department.
This page does not diagnose symptoms or decide whether it is safe to stay at home. You do not need to know which medicine caused a symptom before calling.
Nivolumab helps immune cells act against melanoma. After complete surgery, its aim is to lower the risk of recurrence; this does not guarantee that melanoma will not return.
Nivolumab blocks the PD-1 checkpoint that restrains T cells. The resulting immune activity may control melanoma but can also inflame normal organs. Side effects may first appear after the final dose.
What to watch forCarry your immunotherapy alert card and report new symptoms early, including after treatment ends.
The drawings are simplified explanations of drug action, not anatomical pictures or a prediction of response.
This shows treatment timing, not guaranteed symptom-free days. Your team confirms the active phase and dates.

Nivolumab is given as 240 mg by intravenous (IV) infusion over 30 minutes OR 600 mg by subcutaneous injection over 3–5 minutes, on Day 1 every 2 weeks. Allow extra time for assessment, preparation and observation. The team selects one formulation. A subcutaneous injection is given into the thigh or abdomen, alternating sites and avoiding damaged skin, scars or moles. IV and subcutaneous doses are not interchangeable milligram for milligram. Adjuvant treatment continues for up to 12 months, subject to safety review.
The team confirms treatment dates, recovery and each safety decision. A planned treatment count does not authorise the next dose.
The team supplies actual dates and resolves any source ambiguity. A reference period does not replace a prescription, a local monitoring plan or an individual treatment decision.
Completely resected melanoma with lymph-node involvement or metastatic disease; the team confirms the stage III or resected stage IV indication. Uveal melanoma is excluded from this adjuvant pathway.
Nivolumab every 2 weeks. Adjuvant treatment continues for up to 12 months, subject to safety review.
Bloods and organ safetyNCCP

Blood count, kidney and liver tests, glucose and thyroid tests; review autoimmune conditions, transplants, previous immune reactions and all current medicines. BRAF tumour status is checked for the advanced or adjuvant melanoma indication.

Blood count, kidney/liver tests and glucose before every 2-week cycle. Thyroid function is checked once a month and when clinically indicated. Cortisol and other tests are added when clinically indicated. Report new symptoms at every visit and between visits; normal blood results do not rule out immune toxicity.
Contact the team for new symptoms; extra tests may be needed between scheduled checks.
Safety bloods do not by themselves show whether cancer is responding.

Continue immune-toxicity monitoring for at least five months after the last dose, and longer when advised. Keep any prescribed steroid taper, hormone replacement and specialist follow-up. Scans follow your individual disease plan.
Cancer, skin and daily functionNCCP
Record diagnosis, stage, current disease sites and the baseline assessment.
Keep the source-specific skin and clinical reviews and the individually agreed response assessments.
Record new lesions, lumps, wound changes, pain and effects on usual activities.
Write the next examination or scan date and the responsible team; no universal scan or tumour-marker interval is assumed.
Your stage, symptoms and treatment determine follow-up. Write down the skin and lymph-node checks, any body or brain scans and the service arranging them. Confirm your own dates with the team.
Medicines and continuing precautionsNCCP
Review all medicines and the pregnancy/fertility plan.
Review treatment taken or received, holds, adverse effects and supportive medicines.
Keep the actual urgent contacts and do not restart a held medicine yourself.
Bring the medicine list and treatment summary to other services.

Discuss fertility before starting. Use effective contraception during treatment and for at least 5 months after the last dose. Tell the team promptly about a possible pregnancy. Discuss breastfeeding restrictions with the team before treatment; do not breastfeed without their advice. Do not stop prescribed steroids or hormone replacement yourself.

Allow extra time for assessment, preparation and observation. The team selects one formulation. The team selects one formulation. A subcutaneous injection is given into the thigh or abdomen, alternating sites and avoiding damaged skin, scars or moles. IV and subcutaneous doses are not interchangeable milligram for milligram.

There are no guaranteed “safe days”. The prescribed dose, treatment decision and local urgent-contact plan take priority. Call 112 or 999 for severe breathing difficulty, severe chest pain, collapse, a new seizure, sudden weakness or speech difficulty, or uncontrolled bleeding. Follow your oncology unit’s written urgent-contact plan for other new or worsening symptoms; do not wait for the next appointment.

Nivolumab is given as 240 mg by IV infusion over 30 minutes OR 600 mg by subcutaneous injection over 3–5 minutes, on Day 1 every 2 weeks. Allow extra time for assessment, preparation and observation. The team selects one formulation. A subcutaneous injection is given into the thigh or abdomen, alternating sites and avoiding damaged skin, scars or moles. IV and subcutaneous doses are not interchangeable milligram for milligram. Report symptoms and previous reactions before treatment.

Immunotherapy can cause inflammation in healthy organs during treatment or after it stops. Contact the oncology team promptly for new diarrhoea, blood in stools, cough or breathlessness, yellow skin or eyes, severe headache, vision changes, marked thirst, unusual weakness or a spreading rash. Tell any clinician that you are receiving or have received immunotherapy. Do not wait for the next treatment to report a possible immune effect.
Agree the arrangements with your oncology team.

If a visit is missed or treatment is held, contact the unit for a new plan. Do not count a missed appointment as a dose received. An interval change, operation or new phase does not erase earlier immune toxicity or a permanent-stop decision.
Plan blood tests, travel and medicine collection in advance. If you need an interpreter or someone to help at home, tell the team before the appointment.
Ask for your latest schedule and contact details on paper. Replace old versions when treatment changes so everyone helping you uses the same plan.

Ask which anti-sickness or other symptom medicines are prescribed, when to take them and when to call if they do not help. Do not start a borrowed medicine or alter treatment to manage a side effect yourself.
Keep your actual oncology, out-of-hours and pharmacy contacts on the wallet card. Example numbers on a template must be replaced before you use it.
Let the team know if cramps, altered taste or poor appetite make eating or moving difficult. Ask for practical food and activity advice that fits your symptoms and any other illness.

Some immune effects need steroids or lasting hormone replacement. Follow the exact prescription and taper. Carry the relevant alert information, and do not stop or reduce these medicines yourself when anticancer treatment is held or completed.
Use these questions with your own pathology report and agreed treatment plan.

Record the original melanoma site and pathology findings. Breslow thickness and ulceration describe features of the skin tumour; stage describes its extent. Melanoma arising in the eye or a mucosal surface may need a different pathway.

BRAF V600 testing can identify an alternative targeted-treatment option in some melanomas. It is separate from the immunotherapy described here. Ask what your tumour result means for the choices available to you.
Ask whether medicine is intended to reduce recurrence after complete surgery or control cancer that remains. Add any operation or radiotherapy to the plan with its own purpose, timing and risks.

Stage describes the extent of disease. Response describes a change in measurable cancer during treatment. After complete removal there may be no visible tumour to measure; follow-up then looks for recurrence and treatment effects.
Report a new or changing mole, a sore that persists, a new lump or an unexplained symptom. A photo or a good response in one area cannot rule out a separate problem.
Ask how the medicine fits with previous or planned local treatment. The timing of an operation, radiotherapy and a tablet course should be written in one agreed plan.

A safety pause is an active treatment decision. Record which medicine is paused, the reason, the tests or recovery needed and who may authorise restarting. Do not restart from an old prescription or reset the history when a new phase begins.

If your team has permanently stopped nivolumab because of a serious immune reaction, improvement does not automatically make restarting safe. Keep that decision in your treatment record; only your specialist team can review further treatment.
Keep the written medicine plan beside this guide; it records your own dose and dates.

Show the pharmacist a current list of prescriptions, over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, herbal products and supplements. Include anticoagulants, heart medicines, steroids and recent antibiotics. Check before adding, stopping or changing anything; an apparently harmless product can alter treatment or confuse a symptom assessment.
Bring your medicine list, allergy information and questions. Tell the team about practical problems with travel, swallowing, wound care or remembering doses before treatment starts.
Safety tests, tumour tests and response scans answer different questions.

Ask the team to write the next assessment and who will arrange it. Bloods used to monitor kidneys, liver, hormones or muscle are not automatically measures of cancer response. There is no universal tumour-marker blood schedule for these skin-cancer regimens; a scan or extra blood test is requested for a specific clinical reason.
Keep a named contact for bookings and results. If an expected appointment or result is missing, call that service; do not take silence as confirmation that everything is complete.
You can feel well and still need the planned checks. New symptoms deserve attention even on a day without an appointment.

Record the start and change in symptoms, temperature if advised, bowel pattern, drinking, urine and the effect on normal tasks. A simple few-line record is enough. Use it to describe a change rather than trying to grade or diagnose a toxicity yourself.

Immunotherapy can cause inflammation in healthy organs during treatment or after it stops. Contact the oncology team promptly for new diarrhoea, blood in stools, cough or breathlessness, yellow skin or eyes, severe headache, vision changes, marked thirst, unusual weakness or a spreading rash. Tell any clinician that you are receiving or have received immunotherapy.
Report nausea, mouth discomfort, diarrhoea or weight loss before they make eating and drinking difficult. The team can adjust symptom support and arrange dietitian or rehabilitation advice.
This complements clinical assessment and does not replace it.

Protect exposed skin with clothing, a hat and shade. Use broad-spectrum sunscreen with sun protection factor (SPF) 30 or higher and reapply as directed. Avoid sunbeds. Cloudy weather does not remove ultraviolet exposure.
Ask the team to show you how to check your skin and treated area. Use a mirror or a helper for areas you cannot see. Report a new lump, a changing lesion or a sore that does not heal.

A private, dated photograph can help describe a change if your team finds it useful. Keep the lighting and size reference consistent. Photographs support a discussion; they do not replace examination and need not be uploaded.
Follow the wound and skin-care instructions for the treated area. Ask before adding a cream or remedy. Increasing redness, discharge, pain, bleeding or difficulty using the area needs assessment.
Discuss these precautions before treatment even if pregnancy is not currently planned.

Ask early about fertility preservation, sexual health and symptoms affecting intimacy. Tell the team about any chance of pregnancy, breastfeeding or a partner’s pregnancy so that the correct medicine-specific advice can be given. Keep the precautions and their end dates in the written plan.

Do not share anticancer medicines. Keep oral medicines in their original labelled packaging, away from children and anyone who could take them accidentally. Return unused medicines to the supplying pharmacy and follow its handling advice. A treatment hold does not remove pregnancy precautions.
Your priorities and the burden of treatment belong in the discussion.
Ask what outcome this treatment aims to improve for your diagnosis and what alternatives exist. Results from a study group help a discussion but cannot promise your own result.

Agree the next decision point and what would make the plan change. Ask about other suitable treatments, trials and symptom care. Support for comfort and function can continue alongside cancer treatment.
Tell the team what is hardest in daily life: travel, work, caring duties, costs, sleep or confidence. Ask who can help and how to contact them.
Before going home, check that you can describe your medicine schedule, next tests and urgent-contact route. Ask for an interpreter, larger print or a supporter if that would help.
Keep this record when treatment is paused, changed or completed.

Record the medicines and last dates, important reactions, any long-term hormone replacement or steroid taper, and the responsible oncology contact. Show this information in urgent care and to other specialists. A different treatment phase does not erase earlier toxicity.
Use this handbook as your paper record. Keep the current schedule, medicines, tests and contacts together, and replace outdated pages after a change. The matching QR link is optional.
Discuss the evidence for your diagnosis, tumour test results and treatment setting.

Evidence in advanced melanoma measures control of existing cancer; adjuvant evidence measures recurrence after surgery. Perioperative evidence concerns treatment around surgery. Ask which study and outcome match your stage and plan. These results cannot predict your individual benefit.

Blood count, kidney and liver tests, glucose and thyroid tests; review autoimmune conditions, transplants, previous immune reactions and all current medicines. BRAF tumour status is checked for the advanced or adjuvant melanoma indication. Blood count, kidney/liver tests and glucose before every 2-week cycle. Thyroid function is checked once a month and when clinically indicated. Cortisol and other tests are added when clinically indicated. Report new symptoms at every visit and between visits; normal blood results do not rule out immune toxicity.
Ask the team to enter actual daytime and out-of-hours numbers on the wallet card. Report new symptoms promptly; do not wait for the next appointment.

There are no guaranteed “safe days”. The prescribed dose, treatment decision and local urgent-contact plan take priority. Call 112 or 999 for severe breathing difficulty, severe chest pain, collapse, a new seizure, sudden weakness or speech difficulty, or uncontrolled bleeding. Follow your oncology unit’s written urgent-contact plan for other new or worsening symptoms; do not wait for the next appointment.

Nivolumab is given as 240 mg by IV infusion over 30 minutes OR 600 mg by subcutaneous injection over 3–5 minutes, on Day 1 every 2 weeks. Allow extra time for assessment, preparation and observation. The team selects one formulation. A subcutaneous injection is given into the thigh or abdomen, alternating sites and avoiding damaged skin, scars or moles. IV and subcutaneous doses are not interchangeable milligram for milligram. Report symptoms and previous reactions before treatment.

Immunotherapy can cause inflammation in healthy organs during treatment or after it stops. Contact the oncology team promptly for new diarrhoea, blood in stools, cough or breathlessness, yellow skin or eyes, severe headache, vision changes, marked thirst, unusual weakness or a spreading rash. Tell any clinician that you are receiving or have received immunotherapy. Do not wait for the next treatment to report a possible immune effect.
Agree the arrangements with your oncology team.

If a visit is missed or treatment is held, contact the unit for a new plan. Do not count a missed appointment as a dose received. An interval change, operation or new phase does not erase earlier immune toxicity or a permanent-stop decision.
Plan blood tests, travel and medicine collection in advance. If you need an interpreter or someone to help at home, tell the team before the appointment.
Ask for your latest schedule and contact details on paper. Replace old versions when treatment changes so everyone helping you uses the same plan.

Ask which anti-sickness or other symptom medicines are prescribed, when to take them and when to call if they do not help. Do not start a borrowed medicine or alter treatment to manage a side effect yourself.
Keep your actual oncology, out-of-hours and pharmacy contacts on the wallet card. Example numbers on a template must be replaced before you use it.
Let the team know if cramps, altered taste or poor appetite make eating or moving difficult. Ask for practical food and activity advice that fits your symptoms and any other illness.

Some immune effects need steroids or lasting hormone replacement. Follow the exact prescription and taper. Carry the relevant alert information, and do not stop or reduce these medicines yourself when anticancer treatment is held or completed.
Use these questions with your own pathology report and agreed treatment plan.

Record the original melanoma site and pathology findings. Breslow thickness and ulceration describe features of the skin tumour; stage describes its extent. Melanoma arising in the eye or a mucosal surface may need a different pathway.

BRAF V600 testing can identify an alternative targeted-treatment option in some melanomas. It is separate from the immunotherapy described here. Ask what your tumour result means for the choices available to you.
Ask whether medicine is intended to reduce recurrence after complete surgery or control cancer that remains. Add any operation or radiotherapy to the plan with its own purpose, timing and risks.

Stage describes the extent of disease. Response describes a change in measurable cancer during treatment. After complete removal there may be no visible tumour to measure; follow-up then looks for recurrence and treatment effects.
Report a new or changing mole, a sore that persists, a new lump or an unexplained symptom. A photo or a good response in one area cannot rule out a separate problem.
Ask how the medicine fits with previous or planned local treatment. The timing of an operation, radiotherapy and a tablet course should be written in one agreed plan.

A safety pause is an active treatment decision. Record which medicine is paused, the reason, the tests or recovery needed and who may authorise restarting. Do not restart from an old prescription or reset the history when a new phase begins.

If your team has permanently stopped nivolumab because of a serious immune reaction, improvement does not automatically make restarting safe. Keep that decision in your treatment record; only your specialist team can review further treatment.
Keep the written medicine plan beside this guide; it records your own dose and dates.

Show the pharmacist a current list of prescriptions, over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, herbal products and supplements. Include anticoagulants, heart medicines, steroids and recent antibiotics. Check before adding, stopping or changing anything; an apparently harmless product can alter treatment or confuse a symptom assessment.
Bring your medicine list, allergy information and questions. Tell the team about practical problems with travel, swallowing, wound care or remembering doses before treatment starts.
Safety tests, tumour tests and response scans answer different questions.

Ask the team to write the next assessment and who will arrange it. Bloods used to monitor kidneys, liver, hormones or muscle are not automatically measures of cancer response. There is no universal tumour-marker blood schedule for these skin-cancer regimens; a scan or extra blood test is requested for a specific clinical reason.
Keep a named contact for bookings and results. If an expected appointment or result is missing, call that service; do not take silence as confirmation that everything is complete.
You can feel well and still need the planned checks. New symptoms deserve attention even on a day without an appointment.

Record the start and change in symptoms, temperature if advised, bowel pattern, drinking, urine and the effect on normal tasks. A simple few-line record is enough. Use it to describe a change rather than trying to grade or diagnose a toxicity yourself.

Immunotherapy can cause inflammation in healthy organs during treatment or after it stops. Contact the oncology team promptly for new diarrhoea, blood in stools, cough or breathlessness, yellow skin or eyes, severe headache, vision changes, marked thirst, unusual weakness or a spreading rash. Tell any clinician that you are receiving or have received immunotherapy.
Report nausea, mouth discomfort, diarrhoea or weight loss before they make eating and drinking difficult. The team can adjust symptom support and arrange dietitian or rehabilitation advice.
This complements clinical assessment and does not replace it.

Protect exposed skin with clothing, a hat and shade. Use broad-spectrum sunscreen with sun protection factor (SPF) 30 or higher and reapply as directed. Avoid sunbeds. Cloudy weather does not remove ultraviolet exposure.
Ask the team to show you how to check your skin and treated area. Use a mirror or a helper for areas you cannot see. Report a new lump, a changing lesion or a sore that does not heal.

A private, dated photograph can help describe a change if your team finds it useful. Keep the lighting and size reference consistent. Photographs support a discussion; they do not replace examination and need not be uploaded.
Follow the wound and skin-care instructions for the treated area. Ask before adding a cream or remedy. Increasing redness, discharge, pain, bleeding or difficulty using the area needs assessment.
Discuss these precautions before treatment even if pregnancy is not currently planned.

Ask early about fertility preservation, sexual health and symptoms affecting intimacy. Tell the team about any chance of pregnancy, breastfeeding or a partner’s pregnancy so that the correct medicine-specific advice can be given. Keep the precautions and their end dates in the written plan.

Do not share anticancer medicines. Keep oral medicines in their original labelled packaging, away from children and anyone who could take them accidentally. Return unused medicines to the supplying pharmacy and follow its handling advice. A treatment hold does not remove pregnancy precautions.
Your priorities and the burden of treatment belong in the discussion.
Ask what outcome this treatment aims to improve for your diagnosis and what alternatives exist. Results from a study group help a discussion but cannot promise your own result.

Agree the next decision point and what would make the plan change. Ask about other suitable treatments, trials and symptom care. Support for comfort and function can continue alongside cancer treatment.
Tell the team what is hardest in daily life: travel, work, caring duties, costs, sleep or confidence. Ask who can help and how to contact them.
Before going home, check that you can describe your medicine schedule, next tests and urgent-contact route. Ask for an interpreter, larger print or a supporter if that would help.
Keep this record when treatment is paused, changed or completed.

Record the medicines and last dates, important reactions, any long-term hormone replacement or steroid taper, and the responsible oncology contact. Show this information in urgent care and to other specialists. A different treatment phase does not erase earlier toxicity.
Use this handbook as your paper record. Keep the current schedule, medicines, tests and contacts together, and replace outdated pages after a change. The matching QR link is optional.
Discuss the evidence for your diagnosis, tumour test results and treatment setting.

Evidence in advanced melanoma measures control of existing cancer; adjuvant evidence measures recurrence after surgery. Perioperative evidence concerns treatment around surgery. Ask which study and outcome match your stage and plan. These results cannot predict your individual benefit.

Blood count, kidney and liver tests, glucose and thyroid tests; review autoimmune conditions, transplants, previous immune reactions and all current medicines. BRAF tumour status is checked for the advanced or adjuvant melanoma indication. Blood count, kidney/liver tests and glucose before every 2-week cycle. Thyroid function is checked once a month and when clinically indicated. Cortisol and other tests are added when clinically indicated. Report new symptoms at every visit and between visits; normal blood results do not rule out immune toxicity.
Ask the team to enter actual daytime and out-of-hours numbers on the wallet card. Report new symptoms promptly; do not wait for the next appointment.

unique_source_inventory.text: Severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or severe chest pain: call emergency services. Do not wait for an online answer.

Temperature 37.5°C or higher, 36°C or lower, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell — even with a normal temperature. Contact the oncology team immediately for new or worsening breathlessness, chest pain, persistent diarrhoea, severe tummy pain, yellow skin/eyes, much less urine, severe headache, marked weakness, confusion, unusual thirst or passing much more urine, or a spreading/blistering rash. For severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or other immediately dangerous symptoms, seek emergency care. Do not wait for the next infusion.

Follow the urgent contact instructions from your treating hospital. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Outside clinic hours, use your instructed out-of-hours pathway or the emergency department.
This page does not diagnose symptoms or decide whether it is safe to stay at home. You do not need to know which medicine caused a symptom before calling.
Aim to control advanced lung cancer, relieve symptoms and prolong life where possible.
Nivolumab blocks PD-1 on immune cells, helping them recognise and attack cancer. It can also cause inflammation in healthy organs.
What to watch forReport new breathing, bowel, skin, hormone, heart or nerve symptoms promptly; these may be immune inflammation.

There is no planned chemotherapy induction or maintenance switch in this monotherapy pathway. Treatment is reviewed regularly and may be held, stopped or changed.

There are no guaranteed “safe days”. Immune effects can happen on any day and after treatment ends. Carry your immunotherapy alert card and tell any healthcare team that you receive nivolumab.

The team checks blood results, symptoms and medicines before the prescribed infusion or injection. Tell the nurse immediately about itching, flushing, breathlessness, dizziness or feeling suddenly unwell. Before leaving, confirm the next tests, treatment visit and urgent contact number.

You may feel well between infusions, but immune inflammation can begin at any time. Keep a short symptom record and take medicines exactly as prescribed. Contact your team about new symptoms instead of waiting for your next appointment. Confirm thyroid tests before each cycle and any additional tests your team requests; report new symptoms without waiting for the next treatment.
Agree the arrangements with your oncology team.

Nivolumab 480 mg IV over 60 minutes OR 1200 mg as a subcutaneous injection over 3–5 minutes on Day 1 every 4 weeks. Your team confirms one formulation; the whole visit includes checks and preparation.
Continue until progression or unacceptable toxicity, with individual benefit and safety review.

Blood count, kidney/liver tests and glucose before every 4-week cycle; thyroid function before each cycle and when clinically indicated; cortisol if clinically indicated. Review cancer progression before cycle 4. Continue immune-toxicity monitoring for at least 5 months after the last dose.
Carry your immune alert card, medicine list and urgent contact details. Follow prescribed steroids or hormone replacement carefully; do not stop steroids suddenly.
Keep reporting symptoms and attend agreed follow-up for at least 5 months after the final dose; some hormone replacement continues longer.
Nivolumab alone has minimal sickness risk. Routine preventive anti-sickness medicines or premedication are not usually required; the team may prescribe symptom relief.
Carry your alert card during treatment and afterwards. Show it when seeking urgent care; symptoms can be mistaken for an infection or an ordinary stomach upset.

Some immune effects need steroids or hormone replacement. Follow the prescribed plan and do not stop steroids suddenly. Ask for help if symptoms worsen or you cannot take essential medicines. Hormone replacement alone does not always mean nivolumab must stop. Your team checks symptoms and recovery and reviews any medicines that suppress the immune system before deciding whether treatment can continue or restart.

Discuss pregnancy, fertility and breastfeeding before treatment. Use effective contraception during treatment and for at least 5 months after the last dose. Breastfeeding requires a specialist decision; contact your team promptly if pregnancy occurs.

Nivolumab is given as 480 mg through a vein over 60 minutes OR 1200 mg as an injection under the skin over 3–5 minutes, on Day 1 every 4 weeks. Your team selects one formulation; these doses are not interchangeable milligram for milligram. Allow extra time for safety checks, preparation and observation. Report symptoms and previous reactions before treatment.
Immune side effects may start between visits or after the final dose. Report changes promptly. Follow the support plan and contact oncology early if symptoms develop.
Carry your treatment record, actual urgent contacts and medicine list. Tell the team about line redness, swelling, leakage, pain or fever.

Carry your immune alert card during and after nivolumab. Tell any clinician that you have received immunotherapy. Do not restart a held treatment or change prescribed steroids or hormone replacement yourself.
Tell the team early if swallowing, appetite, pain or taste changes reduce intake. A dietitian can agree practical food, drink or feeding support with you. Do not wait for substantial weight loss.
Agree a mouth-care plan and tell your dentist about previous or current cancer treatment. Arrange oncology advice before dental procedures, particularly after head and neck radiation.
Ask for speech and language therapy if swallowing or speech is difficult. Use the food textures, exercises and communication support advised for you; a general guide cannot establish safe swallowing.

Bring prescribed, over-the-counter and herbal medicines and supplements for review. Discuss fertility preservation and breastfeeding before treatment. Use effective contraception during treatment and for at least five months after the final dose. Tell the team promptly about a possible pregnancy. Do not breastfeed without specific advice from the team.
Keep your own diagnosis and treatment aim at the front of the plan.

Your team weighs the cancer, previous treatment, health, symptoms and preferences when discussing options. Other systemic treatment, local treatment where suitable, trials or symptom-focused care may be discussed.
Cancer treatment can also affect healthy tissue.
Keep one calendar for treatment, tests and other appointments.
Your team may pause or stop treatment to assess side effects. Record the reason, required tests and who can authorise restarting. A new cycle does not erase earlier severe toxicity.

When switching from two-week to four-week dosing, the first four-week dose is given two weeks after the last two-week dose. In the reverse direction, the first two-week dose is given four weeks after the last four-week dose. Your team confirms the actual switch date and formulation.

New cough or breathlessness can signal inflammation or another urgent cause.
Chest pain, racing heartbeat or fainting needs urgent assessment.
Yellow eyes/skin or dark urine may signal inflammation; tests also check the liver.
Report much less urine, new swelling or a change in kidney tests.
New or persistent diarrhoea, blood in stools or severe tummy pain needs urgent advice.
